newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks "sweep" in Northeast, West Coast.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks "sweep" in Northeast, West Coast.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign team spoke confidently on Tuesday of making a "clean sweep" of Northeastern states and the West Coast in the Nov. 5 vote.
Exactly four weeks before Election Day, Clinton was comfortable enough about his lead over Republican Bob Dole to take the day off and muse about playing golf if only the rain would stop.

He returned early on Tuesday from a swing through the heart of New England -- Connecticut, New Hampshire and Maine -- and White House spokesman Mike McCurry said: "We increasingly see the possibility of a clean sweep in the Northeast."

In addition, McCurry said, the Dole campaign's purchases of television advertising in California, Oregon and Washington state suggest he is conceding those West Coast states, where Clinton enjoys substantial polling leads.

"They only have a presence in Calfornia that is sufficient to keep their local folks happy," McCurry claimed. He said Dole is spending about $250,000 a week there but to really contest the state he should spend $1 million or more a week.
The Dole campaign in California sharply disagreed.
"They've been pitching that tall tale for four months now and it's as untrue now as when they first said it," said a Dole spokesman in California, Dale Neugebauer.

"We're running a very competitive campaign here," he said. "We're on the ground all over the state. It's a very aggressive effort. Clinton has a very tough record to defend out here. They may wish we weren't here but we're here, and them saying we're not is just wishful thinking on their part."

The factional sniping over this point underscores the sensitivity of any U.S. presidential candidate -- but especially an underdog like Dole -- letting talk circulate that he has conceded an important state, let alone a region.
Campaign strategists know such talk can demoralise supporters and undercut efforts to mobilise voters not only in the disputed regions but elsewhere.

U.S. presidential elections are decided state-by-state rather than by nationwide popular vote in the indirect U.S. system. A candidate needs a majority of 270 votes in the Electoral College, where votes are apportioned roughly according to state populace. California has the most with 54.

At this point the Clinton campaign considers the states holding the traditional Democratic base sewed up and is turning more attention to areas Democrats have had a hard time winning recently, like Georgia, Florida and Arizona.

For example Clinton will hook up with Vice President Al Gore on Thursday in Knoxville in normally Republican eastern Tennessee to celebrate Gore's Wednesday night debate with Dole's running mate, Jack Kemp.

"We think going into traditionally Republican areas makes the point that this president and this vice president appeal to Democrats and Republicans all across the political spectrum," said Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart.

One aim is to boost to Democratic candidates for Congress. Democrats sense an opportunity to end Republicans' two-year control of the House of Representatives, where they have a 235-198 seat edge with one independent and one seat vacant.
Analysts say the jockeying by campaign strategists will decide less than the issues on which voters make their choice.

"They vote because of the state of the economy, or whether Americans are at peace or getting killed or getting taken hostage," said presidential scholar Stephen Hess of the Brookings Institution. "These are all forces over which the Clinton strategists and Dole strategists have little effect."
His prediction for Nov. 5?
"Clinton's going to win," Hess said. "The legitimate question is how big a victory he has. People who tell you now that he is going to win in a blowout are talking too soon. It can close.
"It won't save Dole but it can save a Republican Congress."
